Because DYNASHIELD operates solely through exposed runtime controls, it requires no retraining or model-internal access. These results suggest that safety-aware dynamic decoding is a promising and practically lightweight defense mechanism for black-box LLM deployments.

title: An Embarrassingly Simple Data Selection Strategy for Million-Scale Multi-Modal Instruction-Tuning
raw_summary: arXiv:2503.13383v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent research demonstrates that pretrained large language models (LLMs) require minimal but carefully curated data for instruction-tuning. Building on LLMs, multi-modal models further contend with far larger data volumes, heterogeneous sources, and cross-modal alignment, amplifying both the necessity and the complexity of data selection. However, existing methods rely on deeply extracted embeddings, gradients or narrow quality scores that are time-consuming to compute and limited in expressiveness, frequently failing to surpass a simple random-sampling baseline. To overcome these limitations, we step back from complex embedding spaces and target the fundamental objective of instruction tuning: how and what knowledge should be elicited from the pretrained model and exposed to users. We leverage interaction \underline{S}tyles as a proxy for structural diversity, and decompose data quality into capability-specific \underline{S}cores, yielding an explicit yet \underline{R}ich (SSR) profile for each sample. We further cast the selection as submodular coverage maximization over the capability--style grid, providing an approximation guarantee. SSR consistently delivers superior performance across two distinct architecture stacks, LLaVA-1.5 (Vicuna + CLIP) and LLaVA-OneVision (Qwen2 + SigLIP), two large-scale data pools, six data budget settings, and 14 multi-modal benchmarks. To our knowledge, SSR is the first data selection method validated at million-scale, achieving 99.1% of full-data performance using only 30% of a 2.6M pool. Furthermore, the SSR profile models and selected subsets transfer training-free across data pools and model architectures with capability extensibility.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Multimodal Consensus for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
raw_summary: arXiv:2510.20256v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) has made considerable progress in recent years. Existing MSA methods mainly learn shared multimodal representations or train unimodal predictors with a common multimodal label. However, assigning the shared label to every modality can obscure modality-specific sentiment, while direct fusion may overemphasize unreliable predictions when modalities disagree. To address these issues, we propose Uncertainty-Guided Multimodal Consensus (UMC), which first recovers continuous unimodal pseudo-labels and then forms a reliability-aware consensus across modalities. Our method consists of two key components: i) Continuous Prototype-Guided Label Recovery (CPLR), which combines heteroscedastic predictions with ordered sentiment prototypes and uses confidence and label conflict to refine continuous unimodal pseudo-labels, and ii) Reliability and Precision Consensus (RPC), which estimates sample-dependent modality reliability from predictive statistics and cross-modal disagreement and combines it with predictive precision through a closed-form consensus solver. Extensive experiments conducted on four publicly available MSA datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed model.

title: Cross-User Poisoning: User-Task Boundary Failures in Multi-User Collaborative Language Agents
raw_summary: arXiv:2511.17671v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language agents are moving from single-user assistants to shared collaborators in workspaces, forums, and group chats. A shared agent observes interleaved messages from multiple users, maintains persistent context, and executes tool actions, creating a boundary problem absent from standard single-user agents: the agent must decide not only whether an instruction is safe, but which user or task it is allowed to govern. We identify cross-user poisoning (CUP), where an adversary injects a message into shared context that is later applied while the agent serves a benign user, causing unauthorized actions or responses outside the instruction's intended scope. We validate CUP on two deployed multi-user agents, Continua and ElizaOS, and introduce MURMUR, a framework for evaluating shared-context agents under concurrent multi-user interactions. Across Slack, Workspace, and Airline domains, CUP achieves high attack success, persists across later interactions, and remains substantially more effective than matched prompt-injection attacks. We evaluate boundary-scoping defenses and find that context summarization alone is insufficient, while task clustering and provenance prompting substantially reduce non-adaptive propagation. These results show that robust multi-user agents require explicit user/task scoping rather than generic input filtering or context compression.

title: SELF: A Robust Singular Value and Eigenvalue Approach for LLM Fingerprinting
raw_summary: arXiv:2512.03620v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safeguarding the Intellectual Property (IP) of Large Language Models (LLMs) against model theft represents a critical challenge in contemporary AI research. Although fingerprinting is essential for establishing forensic evidence for model derivation, existing methods are susceptible to false claim attacks, weight manipulations, or high false positive rates, undermining their utility. To overcome these limitations, we propose SELF, \rev{a novel intrinsic weight-based fingerprinting scheme tailored for robust IP forensics via adversarial model lineage verification}. SELF eliminates dependency on input and inherently resists false claims, achieving robust \rev{provenance detection} through unique, scalable and transformation-invariant fingerprint extraction via singular value and eigenvalue decomposition of LLM attention weights. Experimental results demonstrate that SELF maintains high IP infringement detection accuracy while significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in reducing false positives and showing strong robustness against various downstream modifications, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/HanxiuZhang/SELF_v4.

title: Scaling Reasoning Efficiently via Relaxed On-Policy Distillation
raw_summary: arXiv:2603.11137v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for transferring reasoning capabilities to capacity-constrained models, yet sampled-token OPD often suffers from entropy collapse and negative transfer. We identify uniform credit allocation as a key bottleneck: existing objectives obtain dense teacher feedback on student-generated trajectories, but apply it uniformly across sampled tokens despite highly heterogeneous token-level signals. Most tokens carry redundant near-zero credit, while rare heavy-tailed negative credits can dominate updates and prematurely suppress plausible reasoning trajectories. We introduce REOPOLD (Relaxed On-Policy Distillation), a framework that relaxes this uniform assignment by controlling where teacher feedback is applied, how strongly it affects the update, and when the allocation rule changes during training. Across diverse reasoning tasks, REOPOLD improves sampled-token OPD over recent post-training baselines with up to 12x higher sample efficiency, and extends to cross-vocabulary distillation, self-distillation, and test-time scaling.

title: Decoupling and Regulating Modality Heads for Fake News Detection under Missing Modality
raw_summary: arXiv:2604.09711v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal news often loses its image or text as it spreads across Web platforms. Existing methods treat this as information loss, assuming that the original veracity label remains valid. This assumption fails for fake news reusing authentic material, whose remainder may be genuine. Detectors should therefore decouple modality cues and adapt their contributions to modality availability. However, coarse news labels provide little guidance for modality decoupling, while training on complete inputs can induce modality bias. To address these challenges, we propose Head-wise Modality Decoupling and Regulation (HMDR) for multimodal large language models. First, Modality Head Decoupling decouples modality representations through soft head grouping by attention preference. Second, Modality Head Regulation regulates head contributions through compensation for imbalanced modality attention. Finally, Modality Invariance Learning promotes invariance by aligning representations of each modality under replacement of the other. Experiments on two benchmarks show that HMDR improves detection under missing modalities while maintaining performance on complete inputs.

title: Who Gets Flagged? The Pluralistic Evaluation Gap in AI Content Watermarking
raw_summary: arXiv:2604.13776v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Watermarking is becoming the default mechanism for AI content authentication, with governance policies and frameworks referencing it as infrastructure for content provenance. Yet across text, image, and audio modalities, watermark signal strength, detectability, and robustness depend on statistical properties of the content itself, properties that vary systematically across languages, cultural visual traditions, and demographic groups. We examine how this content dependence creates modality-specific pathways to bias. Reviewing the major watermarking benchmarks across modalities, we find that, with one exception, none report performance across languages, cultural content types, or population groups. To address this, we propose three concrete evaluation dimensions for pluralistic watermark benchmarking: cross-lingual detection parity, culturally diverse content coverage, and demographic disaggregation of detection metrics. We argue that watermarking is part of the pluralistic alignment pipeline and should be held to the same evaluation standards. We connect this to governance frameworks currently mandating watermarking deployment without requiring fairness evaluation. Our position is that evaluation must precede deployment, and that the same bias auditing requirements applied to AI models should extend to the verification layer.

title: Clinical Note Bloat Reduction for Efficient LLM Use
raw_summary: arXiv:2604.16364v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Background: Clinical notes contain extensive duplicated text from templates, copy-paste, and auto-populated fields ("note bloat"), diluting clinical signal, limiting longitudinal context, and increasing large language model (LLM) costs. Methods: TRACE removes note bloat using note-level EHR metadata to identify templated and copied content, with frequency-based de-duplication when metadata are unavailable. We evaluated TRACE using blinded physician span review and gold-standard templated-text annotations across four cohorts spanning liver transplant, obstetrics, and inpatient populations at multiple health systems (5.3M notes). We compared zero-shot LLMs and embedding-based classifiers using original and TRACE-processed notes for 20 information extraction tasks and prediction of 5-year survival, postpartum hemorrhage, and 30-day readmission. Results: Only 0.3-6.6% of removed text was flagged as author-generated; TRACE captured 86% of annotated templated characters. Information extraction F1 differences averaged by cohort ranged from -0.009 to +0.004; task-specific prediction F1 differences ranged from -0.011 to +0.018. Among 1,000 randomly sampled Stanford Health Care patients, TRACE reduced chart text by 47.3% (742.7M characters), averaging 220,167 fewer tokens per patient. Using 2024 encounter volumes at a large tertiary academic center and one query per encounter, projected three-year net savings ranged from $1.00M to $13.58M across evaluated model pricing schemes, including initial and annual TRACE processing costs. Conclusion: TRACE substantially reduces clinical note redundancy while preserving information extraction and prediction performance. Underused EHR metadata can reduce LLM inference costs, expand usable longitudinal context, and support scalable clinical AI.

title: ShredBench: Evaluating the Semantic Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs in Document Reconstruction
raw_summary: arXiv:2604.23813v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable performance in Visually Rich Document Understanding (VRDU) tasks, but their capabilities are mainly evaluated on pristine, well-structured document images. We consider content restoration from shredded fragments, a challenging VRDU setting that requires integrating visual pattern recognition with semantic reasoning under significant content discontinuities. To facilitate systematic evaluation of complex VRDU tasks, we introduce ShredBench, a benchmark supported by an automated generation pipeline that renders fragmented documents directly from Markdown. The proposed pipeline ensures evaluation validity by allowing the flexible integration of latest or unseen textual sources to prevent training data contamination. ShredBench assesses four scenarios (English, Chinese, Code, Table) with three fragmentation granularities (8, 12, 16 pieces). Empirical evaluations on state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal a significant performance gap: The method is effective on intact documents; however, once the document is shredded, restoration becomes a significant challenge, with NED dropping sharply as fragmentation increases. Our findings highlight that current MLLMs lack the fine-grained cross-modal reasoning required to bridge visual discontinuities, identifying a critical gap in robust VRDU research.

title: Rethinking State Tracking in Recurrent Models Through Error Control Dynamics
raw_summary: arXiv:2605.07755v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The theory of state tracking in recurrent architectures has predominantly focused on expressive capacity: whether a fixed architecture can theoretically realize a set of symbolic transition rules. We argue that equally important is error control, the dynamics governing hidden-state drift along the directions that distinguish symbolic states. We prove that affine recurrent networks, a class of models encompassing State-Space Models and Linear Attention, cannot correct errors along state-separating subspaces once they preserve state representations. Consequently, practical affine trackers do not learn robust state tracking; rather, they learn finite-horizon solutions governed by accumulated state-relevant error. We characterize the mechanics of this failure, showing that tracking remains readable only while the accumulating within-class spread remains small relative to the between-class separation. We demonstrate empirically on group state-tracking tasks that this breakdown is predictable: tracking collapses when the distinguishability ratio crosses the readability threshold. Across trained models, the point of this crossing predicts the horizon at which downstream accuracy fails. These results establish that robust state tracking is determined not only by an architecture's theoretical expressivity but crucially by its error control.

title: The Geometry of Learning: Read-Write Asymmetry Across Training
raw_summary: arXiv:2605.16600v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pretraining and alignment update the same transformer weights, and we ask in which directions each stage changes them. The residual stream gives every matrix a shared coordinate system, in which a weight change can be compared with the principal subspace of the activations the matrix reads and with the prediction subspace of the unembedding. In this frame, alignment updates to the query and key matrices are enriched in the principal input subspace, while its updates to the output matrices are close to random relative to the prediction subspace, and the same signature appears in late pretraining and under every objective we apply to one checkpoint, so it is a property of the training stage rather than of the objective. The gradient of a linear map is a sum of outer products $\delta_t a_t^\top$, and the residual stream enters this product through the activation $a_t$ for matrices that read from it and through the upstream gradient $\delta_t$ for matrices that write into it. Read gradients therefore inherit the spectrum of the activations, which is the same under every objective, while write gradients inherit the geometry of the upstream gradients, which point into the prediction subspace only early in pretraining, when the output matrices acquire their prediction geometry. The raw read gradient follows the activation spectrum, the optimiser attenuates the concentration it inherits, and cancellation between tokens sets the scale of the update but not its direction. A write direction derived from the unembedding still changes predictions after alignment, and adaptation restricted to any single group of matrices remains effective, so the signature describes where training places its updates, not which matrices can carry them.

title: Strong Teacher Not Needed? On Distillation in LLM Pretraining
raw_summary: arXiv:2605.23857v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge distillation generally assumes a strong-to-weak relationship where stronger teachers yield better students. In this work, we examine this assumption about distillation in large language model pretraining. By varying architecture sizes and training token budgets, we create strong-to-weak, same-level, and weak-to-strong teacher-student relationships, and study distillation's effectiveness under each. We find that the teacher need not be strong: with proper mixing of the language modeling and knowledge distillation losses, even small and undertrained teachers improve larger students. At the same time, a stronger teacher is not always better: pushing the teacher further, through more parameters or more training tokens, can saturate or even reverse the distillation gains. We further observe that distillation improves generalization (out-of-distribution and downstream performance) more readily than in-domain fitting. Together, these results challenge the common belief that distillation pretraining always requires a strong teacher.

title: Spatio-Temporal Audio Language Modeling for Dynamic Sound Sources
raw_summary: arXiv:2606.14141v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sound events have semantic identities, locations, and trajectories, yet existing audio-language models typically encode clips as global event content. Conversely, sound event localization models track source directions over time but offer limited semantic coverage for language reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce ST-AudioQA, a spatio-temporal audio QA dataset and benchmark built from first-order ambisonic (FOA) renderings of static and moving sound sources. Each scene provides source identity, activity, direction, distance, and motion metadata, enabling dense trajectory supervision and QA about what is sounding, where it is, how it moves, and how sources relate. We further introduce ST-Audio Encoder, which jointly learns event semantics and time-resolved source trajectories, and ST-AudioLM, which exposes these audio tokens to an LLM for spatio-temporal audio QA. Experiments show that this representation improves the balance between semantic preservation and localization and yields stronger reasoning than static spatial and localization-oriented baselines. Beyond the controlled benchmark, ST-AudioLM shows zero-shot transfer to real recordings, with further gains after light adaptation. Project page: https://st-audiolm.github.io/.

title: Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge
raw_summary: arXiv:2608.29249v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The online culinary ecosystem is increasingly populated by recipe content generated, modified, or summarized by LLMs. Although often convincing, such outputs may contain hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we present a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted from informal culinary sources and augmented by LLMs. Developed as part of FKG(.in), a knowledge graph of Indian food, the pipeline identifies and addresses common failure modes, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from the source text, through a multi-stage process combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification. Although evaluated on Indian recipes, the proposed methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains. We provide a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic approach to improving the reliability of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

title: Choosing Coding-Agent Benchmarks for Practice: Lessons from Task Demands and Agent Behaviour
raw_summary: arXiv:2609.01271v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Software teams evaluating coding agents need evidence that reflects the changes they expect those agents to make. Benchmark scores summarize how often an agent resolves tasks under broad labels such as bug fixing and feature implementation, but provide little guidance on whether the evaluated work resembles a team's workload. To support this decision, we characterize 2,487 tasks from five public benchmarks and analyze 14,922 runs of six agent configurations. We introduce the Spread-Novelty-Centrality (SNC) profile to describe how the reference solution is distributed across files and directories, how much it adds relative to what it removes, and the dependencies, history, and complexity of the code it touches. We also compare the scope of agent patches and their file exploration. Every pair of benchmarks differs on at least two SNC axes, including benchmarks with the same task label. Among tasks resolved by Claude Opus 4.6, patches are larger than the reference on FeatBench and smaller on FeatureBench. Across the six configurations, resolved runs tend to involve less distributed changes and code with lower values on the Centrality indicators, while the patch sizes associated with resolution differ between the Claude and Qwen configurations. These observations suggest that practitioners should select evaluation tasks based on their change characteristics, inspect the information provided in task descriptions, and assess patch scope alongside test outcomes. We explain how teams can apply this analysis to completed changes and identify the additional evidence needed before using it for task assignment or review automation.

title: EvoIn: Bridging Evolution and Internalization for Agent Fine-Tuning
raw_summary: arXiv:2609.35290v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work has explored improving agents by jointly evolving their harnesses and models, but often takes a ''potpourri'' approach that bundles together new tools, new decision-making procedures, and model adaptation to the evolved harness under a single notion of agent improvement. In this paper, we instead investigate how agents can improve their decision-making procedures. In particular, we propose EvoIn, an agent fine-tuning framework that bridges evolution and internalization. EvoIn first analyzes agent execution traces to evolve and validate new decision-making procedures by temporarily instantiating them in the harness. The validated procedures guide the agent to generate improved reasoning traces. These traces are then rewritten into self-contained reasoning traces, removing explicit references to harness instructions while expressing the induced decision logic as the model's own reasoning. Finally, EvoIn fine-tunes the model on the rewritten traces, internalizing these procedures so that the improved decision-making persists without the evolved harness at inference time. We evaluate EvoIn on diverse benchmarks and find that it consistently enables agents to learn stronger decision-making procedures, raising the pass rate by 10.9 points in-domain and by 9.2 points out-of-domain. Results further show that the internalized decision procedures generalize to unseen tasks. Case studies show that agents can learn to decide how to solve a task before solving it, for example by checking a document's length to choose between reading it in full and searching it. EvoIn is also broadly applicable, showing consistent improvements on another model family.

title: Lost in the bf16 Cast: Exporting Ternary Language Models Can Revert Most Low-Learning-Rate Code Changes
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.07853v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ternary language models such as BitNet b1.58, Falcon-E and BitCPM are fine-tuned through higher-precision latents and deployed as ternary codes by an export that, in the labs' documented pipelines, first casts latents to bf16. We audit releases from three labs. In released checkpoints, fp32 quantization of the shipped latents disagrees with deployed codes on 0.83-1.77% of codes (Falcon-E, BitCPM) and 1.530% (2B-4T); most Falcon-E and BitCPM disagreements are bf16 products exactly on the threshold, which ties-to-even maps to zero, and the unmodified onebitllms exporter reproduces all four Falcon-E releases byte for byte. At fine-tuned endpoints with ULP-matched rates, the documented export lowers greedy GSM8K strict accuracy from 58.79% to 0.78% (Falcon-E-1B-Base) and 36.13% to 0.39% (BitCPM-CANN-0.5B), and a bf16 save and reload lowers 2B-4T's by 27.54 points while its last-number accuracy rises at that endpoint. The strict decrease recurs at each of three new seeds in all three models and has the same direction on 607 reserve test rows, but it is recipe-dependent: at Falcon-E's online-loss-selected rate the export was non-inferior, and after a longer recipe no difference was detected. Two remedies, writing the trained codes directly or adjusting bf16 inputs so unchanged tools emit them, met an inherited 4-point strict-accuracy non-inferiority criterion in all three models, also for the pooled mean over three fixed new trajectories per model and, separately, on the reserve rows. In a frozen study of bf16 latents in fine-tuning (one task, one trajectory per arm), native bf16 writes left 2B-4T's endpoint codes unchanged and changed one Falcon-E code; emulated stochastic-rounding and compensated writers changed codes and were non-inferior to fp32 training at that margin. In two model families, randomized threshold-distance interventions support distance-dependent selection of changed codes.

title: Attention-Graph Curvature for the Verification of Mathematical Reasoning
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.16709v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language models have recently solved open Erd\H{o}s problems and achieved gold-medal level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. But their solutions, written in natural language, cannot yet be verified by proof assistants. An erroneous reasoning step can invalidate every step that comes after, so it is advantageous to detect errors early. Several methods have been proposed to detect erroneous reasoning quickly based on the features of the forward pass of the language model that performs reasoning. In this work, we study whether the directed Forman curvature of that model's attention graph, a local quantity computed at an edge from the attention weights around it, carries information about a step's correctness. To do so, we evaluate four per-step verifiers on ProcessBench with and without the curvature appended to their input. Appending curvature values improves the overall mean performance of all four verifiers. ReProbe, the verifier that takes every token of a step as input, shows the largest improvement. Adding the curvature increases the time of the language model's forward pass by 18% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/kanghyeonz/attention-graph-curvature.

title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.23284v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.

title: Where Does Rhetorical Distortion Live? A Multi-Platform, Multi-Language Measurement of Influencer Content
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.26412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Much of the manipulation in influencer content is not false but disproportionate, framing accurate facts as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Existing approaches either verify factual claims or detect clickbait and propaganda in single-platform, single-language text; however, they overlook where such framing originates, because they treat a post and the replies beneath it as one unit. To address this gap, we measure rhetorical distortion with one instrument applied identically across six platforms and two languages, classifying creator posts and their replies separately. Our three-tier pipeline detects five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion): bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false positives, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. This design keeps labels transparent and comparable across platforms, calls the LLM on only 14% of posts, and supports validation against human annotators and a second model. On 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter, platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (partial $\eta^2=0.49$ vs. $0.09$), and X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). On X/Twitter, the top-5 replies under a post carry 3.5x the distortion of the tweet they answer (1.5x at equal length), while creator tweets alone are indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky; two human annotators and GPT-4o confirm this gap. Measured distortion on threaded platforms thus lives largely in the audience layer, which calls for measuring creator and reply text separately.

title: Knowing When to Stop: The Evidence-Action Gap in Coding Agents
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.31895v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding agents are trained to complete tasks, and they keep trying even when the environment makes completion impossible. The evidence that only outside help can restore progress usually appears within a few steps, yet agents rarely act on it: they over-persist, attempt undesired workarounds, and claim success the record does not support -- a phenomenon we call evidence-action gap. To measure it, we introduce ImpasseBench, which injects twelve realistic environment blockers into otherwise solvable repair tasks and marks, in each trajectory, the step at which the collected evidence becomes sufficient. Scoring actions relative to that step separates appropriate effort from over-persistence and premature handoff. Across eight frontier models and 19,371 trajectories, we find that nearly every run that needs outside help collects sufficient evidence, yet a third still exhaust their budget, and every unsafe request we detect comes after that point. Fortunately, an escalation tool, or an external monitor for models that ignore the tool, already guards against much of this behavior: the tool cuts budget exhaustion from 34.0% to 6.7%, and the monitor nearly triples task success after environment restoration. Even then, a fired escalation is not yet a useful handoff: tickets reliably name the blocker but often omit the agent's own progress and verification status. Taken together, we argue that knowing when to stop therefore needs explicit support, both in the tool that lets an agent hand off and in the report it leaves behind.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.35715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones. These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.

GitHub Octoverse 2026
raw_summary: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
raw_summary: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave". Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well. Battle Drones This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already…

title: Quoting Terk Terkowitz
raw_summary: If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. title: GPT-6.1 Terra
raw_summary: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. Here are the pelicans for the different reasoning levels. This pelican for "max" cost 11.3161 cents and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds: Here's a new comparison grid showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier lineup: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna. GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1/million input tokens and $5/million output - almost half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and around 10x the price of GPT-6 Luna. Via Hacker News Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , gpt

title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
raw_summary: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

title: How to Learn ML in 2026 interview
raw_summary: I had the pleasure of being interviewed by Yacine of Deep Learning with Yacine . He posed a lot of very thoughtful questions and I had a great time. Please check it out! The lightly edited transcript follows, auto-transcribed with faster-whisper and then reviewed by me for correctness, adding links for context, and editing out a lot of “I think” and “um” and “like” selectively. (Yacine) A lot of people asked me how to get into machine learning in 2026. Instead of giving you my usual advice, I figured it’d be way more interesting to sit down with expert contributors who have like a diverse background and ask them what do you think about that. So today we’re chatting with the legendary Vicki Boykis. She’s an absolute gem if you know her from Twitter and Bluesky at giving well-grounded advice that are full of pragmatism. She has a pretty impressive career so far. She built a recommendation system at Tumblr. She worked on the ML platform at Duo Security. She worked on LLMs at Mozilla.ai and today she’s a founding ML engineer at Malachyte, a New York startup doing real-time search and personalization for e-commerce. The cool thing is that she’s actually self-taught and actually started with a degree in economics. Her first job was in trade consulting which she described as just doing a lot of Excel spreadsheet stuff. Then she noticed her co-worker automating their analysis with R and SAS which I haven’t heard in a long time. And she asked herself how do I do that too. That question, how do I do that, pretty much drove our entire career. After first asking herself that, she then did an analytic outcome cast, then she went into data science and then machine learning engineering. Every time she saw someone one step further down this machine learning kind of career pipeline, she went and learned what they were doing on their own and then internalized that skill. So I asked her this simple question which is if you were starting learning this stuff in 2026, how would you actually do it? It was a very insightful and pragmatic conversation and I hope you enjoy it. (Vicki) I graduated with a B. S. in Economics. So nothing to do with machine learning or programming. I started working in analytics and international trade consulting, which is a fancy word for saying I did a lot of Excel spreadsheets. I saw my co-workers were using this thing called R. Oh God, that’s so long ago. R and SAS to automate some of the analysis we were doing. I’m like, how do I do more of that? I want to be able to control things. And then from there, I moved into data analytics and worked at a few places like Comcast, also working on some of their recommendations and then more into data science. And when I was doing data science, I saw that people were actually getting data programmatically themselves. And I’m like, okay, I can analyze the data. How do I actually get that data? So that’s when I moved more into machine learning engineering, which is the process of synthesizing the data, being able to ship it. And then I saw that people were not only building models, but they were shipping it to production. I’m like, how do I do more of that? So my whole career has been about moving towards doing more and more and more of that process myself. And I think that’s pretty reflective of where the industry has been headed in general, right? So we started out with data science or with analytics, with bespoke packages, bespoke models. And now we’re at the point where we’re running enormous clusters that are running LLMs. And now we have inference engineering as the hottest topic. So I think my career fairly mirrors that. So like I said, I’ve worked at Comcast. I got into the recommendations and search space completely by accident, I think, as a lot of people do. I love it. I love working on search and recommendations. I worked on recommendations for Tumblr , which is an old school social network. Then I worked on ML platforms at Duo. I worked on LLMs at Mozilla.ai . And right now I work at Malachyte, which is a startup based in New York doing search and recommendations and real time personalization for e-commerce. So, it kind of echoes of the same thing that I’ve been doing. (Yacine) But for e-commerce merchants specifically and personalizing their stuff in real time. So cool. And I feel like every time I ask somebody, like how they got started with them, they never, it’s very rare that somebody went to, oh yeah, I did a bachelor in machine learning. Like they usually come from all over the place. In my case, I’m from neuroscience. So like I had to pick up like machine learning because I was like, how the hell I’m going to do like all these stats on like these data sets. There’s just no way. And then they were so like complex that I had to programmatically like interact with them in some shape or form. And I had to run them on the Slurm, with Slurm on the cluster. So I had no choice, right? Otherwise, like I’m not going to get the work done. But then you start to, I don’t know, I feel like once you start to kind of realize what you can do with it, it’s kind of like something like a facet of programming that just appear, right? A bit like before you know programming, you’re like, you don’t know, like that you can automate stuff deterministically, then you learn maybe about like functional programming, like object oriented, there’s different ways of thinking about that. But then you learn about like machine learning, where you have like this black box, and then you can feed it data, and then the output that you want, and it will automate this without you having to like define it. So do you feel like machine learning is more of a set of tools and skills than like a career, per se? (Vicki) It certainly seems like it’s becoming more of that. I think like we have a lot more blending, because machine learning used to be, like you said, very much a black box, right? It just kind of sits over there. And there’s even a paper about it, which is not machine learning is the high interest credit card of technical debt . But there’s another one that says like the model is the black box . And basically all the parts of the machine learning system are around it. And you don’t know what’s in it. But now what’s happened is like everybody has access to this model, right? Everybody has access to the API. And so we don’t necessarily have access to what’s inside of it. But at least more of that has been exposed and is now being synthesized in products a lot, a lot more than it used to be. So it definitely feels like it’s become more of a tool that you need to learn. At the same time, like with my own biases of working with a lot of these larger systems, is that these systems also themselves have gotten bigger and have integrated more of like, allows in those traditional tools. And I think the big question I want to ask here, and I have a whole bunch of others, but like the big question is like, what do you think like, in 2026, someone that wants to learn like mastering or deep learning should be doing right? And let’s say it was you, like, back in the days, and now you realize that there’s this whole thing, what would you do? (Vicki) Yeah, this is a big caveat. title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
raw_summary: Interesting research: “ AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities ” Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses...

title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: Unsolicited Opinions
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : Unsupported assertions, accumulated over many years in my drafts folder, last updated in early 2022, now more or less painful in retrospect. In no particular order, except where they are. I will not elaborate or explain. "The Tyranny of Structurelessness" explains a hell of a lot about modern life. If the problem is that powerful people are not accountable for their actions, network forms of organization are the very opposite of solutions. Increasing returns $\Rightarrow$ monopolistic competition $\Rightarrow$ market failure explains a hell of a lot about modern life. Endogamy systematically confounds genetic and cultural inheritance. It would be astonishing if personal-level variables which are entirely the product of social structure, custom, tradition, and strategic action weren't genetically predictable. During the 20th century, and in much of the world even today, genetic variation in resistance to lead poisoning during brain development would, psychometrically, look like a heritable general intelligence. Multiculturalists who expect different cultural groups to have different values and standards of excellence should not expect those groups to be equally represented in all occupations and professions, especially if people are free to enter and leave different lines of work. There is a branch of the wave-function where Margaret Thatcher (trained research chemist and honorary FRS) led a successful push by the international community to address global warming through carbon pricing. (This probably require postponing the collapse of the Soviet bloc by at least a few years, so that her major speech to the UN about the urgency of tackling global warming didn't happen right before the Berlin Wall came down.) In that timeline, pollution charges are regarded as one of the signature policies of neoliberalism. Modern civilization may be doomed because (i) we need to act collectively and globally on climate change, (ii) the USA is the indispensable nation at the center of the network, (iii) the Senate and Electoral College give a veto over American policy to a combination of plutocracy, reactionary folk Christianity and paranoia, and (iv) people like me are unwilling to move to Wyoming, or even West Virginia, to counter this. (I realize there is some tension between this and the previous statement.) A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. The quantitative social sciences would be in much better shape if the first method everyone learned was $k$-nearest-neighbors , or maybe classification and regression trees , followed by the bootstrap . Linear models and $t$-tests should be, for social scientists , the hyper-mathematical arcana at the back of the textbook which their methods class skipped because there wasn't time. "Prophesying upon the eigenvectors" is more transparently about making stuff up than "interpreting the coefficients", and therefore preferable. There is something very odd about looking at the distribution of node degrees within a network. It makes the network itself into an odd hybrid of a single interdependent object (a relation) and a whole population. Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. A good philosophy of probability should explain why all applied Bayesian statistics relies on Monte Carlo, the most frequentist method imaginable. Ideally, it would also explain why Monte Carlo works with deterministic pseudo-random number generators (so the algorithmic information content of the pseudo-random numbers is extremely low). I have toyed for years with the phrases "the simulation interpretation of probability" and "the birth of Trumpism out of the spirit of fandom", but I cannot work out what should stand behind them. (I hope they are unrelated.) Complexity science is a series of footnotes to Norbert Wiener and Herbert Simon . The mythopoetic impulse never goes away , but in populations which have gone through the Flynn / Gellner transition to widespread clerk-ship, it expresses itself not as stories, but as theories which aren't actually explanatory. (It gives us the Oedipus complex, rather than Oedipus.) Every form of progress has its costs. Believing that there was a unique and irreversible transition from viewing time as an eternal cycle to viewing time as unidrectional history is taking sides. His ideas are flawed by a vicious circle; you are engaged in iterative approximation; I stand firm at a fixed point. Dentists are not, in fact, talking their book when they recommend pre-emptive action for wisdom teeth. In a well-functioning social institution, incentives, information and (internalized) norms ensure that it doesn't matter who fills various roles in the institution, it behaves the same way regardless. Institutions are always impersonal. It follows that institutions are information-hiding abstractions, if we're thinking like programmers. But if we're thinking like physicists: institutions are collective degrees of freedom. Blackouts are humanity confronting its own work, and the effects of its own collective actions, as a hostile and alien force. The parable of the Nazi bar is a folk version of the Schelling model . No one should be allowed to opine about artificial intelligence unless they've at least spent an hour or two with ELIZA and then stepped through the code. "Philip K. Dick and the Fake Humans" doesn't yet explain a hell of a lot about modern life, but it will.

title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product.
